speechtext: In view of the very important statements made yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), will the government give the house an early opportunity of discussing this all-important question of the general policy of marketing our wheat crop, I Would suggest not later than Monday next? speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WHEAT POLICY AND IMPLEMENTING LEGISLATION -WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
Speaking for the government I would say that we regard: the war appropriation bill as the most important measure to be brought before the house, and we intend to continue with a consideration of that measure until it is passed, after which other legislation will be taken up. As to Whether or not there will be legislation based upon the statements made yesterday, as my hon. friend knows the intention of 'the government in these matters will be made known when the legislation itself is brought down.
I should like to make clear to my hon. friend and to other members of the house [DOT]that the government naturally is anxious as far as possible to oblige hon. members with respect to the order of proceedings, as well as all else; but I should like the house to know why the government is anxious to dispose of this war appropriation measure as quickly as possible. I do not think I need say anything other 'than to remind hon. members of the situation with which the world may be faced at any moment. I would point out that the ministers who are particularly concerned with the war appropriation measure are the ones who are most responsible for the measures to be taken at a time of war, and that all of them are obliged to be continuously in the house While this measure is under discussion. The ministers include the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Defence for Air, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National War Services. All these hon. gentlemen head: departments which are immediately concerned with matters pertaining to the war, and except for the forenoon, when they are also obliged for part of the morning to attend meetings of the cabinet, they have no opportunity to discuss matters with itheir own officials. Moreover, they are all members of the war committee of the cabinet and are obliged to give their time to its proceedings as well.
Business oj the House

The purpose of the government to continue the discussion on this measure until it is completed, without having discussion upon any other measure intervene, is actuated by our belief that the debate will conclude more quickly if we do not interrupt it to bring in otiher subjects for discussion, but ratlher 001m tinue the present discussion until the measure is passed. Then the members of the government I have mentioned will enjoy a little more freedom, and- will be able to give the attention which is very necessary alt this time to various matters in the departments with which they are immediately concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: WHEAT POLICY AND IMPLEMENTING LEGISLATION -WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make an
observation with respect to the statement just made by the Prime Minister. It is apparent, I think, that the war appropriation measure is the most important measure on the agenda for this session. But may I point out to the Prime Minister and to the house that this measure is for 'the succeeding fiscal year. We 'have 'been told by the Minister of Finance that supplementary appropriations will have to be made for the current fiscal year. I am astonished that that w>as not 'brought in before this measure was introduced.
There can be no immediate need for the passage of 'this resolution and the bill to be based on it, because in any event it would not be available until after the first of April. May I point out to the Prime Minister that a suggestion was made to one of his colleagues that if the government would facilitate the discussion on agriculture it would have the probable effect of facilitating the passage of this resolution. I am advised that that offer was rejected. I think that is quite apparent, because the 'action of 'the minister has been to insist upon the passage of this resolution. I suggest to the Prime Minister and to members of the government, and ask them to take the suggestion into consideration, that if they will facilitate the discussion of the important matter of agriculture they will go a long way toward forwarding their own position with respect to this war appropriation resolution.
We cannot compel that. We ask it, as a matter of public convenience to members on this side of the bouse, as well as members on the other side of the bouse. There is not the pressing necessity for the passage of this war appropriation resolution that there was at the last session. It will be recalled that at the last session the resolution covering $700,000,000 was passed with little or no discussion. We did everything we could to facilitate it. That could not happen again, having regard to public opinion in this country. We would

be derelict in our duty if we did not investigate the manner in which the money has been expended under that bill, and the moneys that are to be spent under this resolution. I suggest to the ministry that this is a world of give and take. We have facilitated the government's war measures on every occasion. We 'have arrived at the position now where the government say the opposition has no rights in this house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WHEAT POLICY AND IMPLEMENTING LEGISLATION -WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has missed altogether, the purport of my remarks. It is not a question of when the money will be needed under this appropriation measure. That is not the question with which the government is concerned at this time. What we are concerned with is that the house enable the ministers of defence, the Minister of Finance and others I have mentioned, and who are obliged to be here while this measure is being discussed, to reach as soon as possible a point where their minds may be free of the measure, and where they can devote their time to other very pressing matters.
We have been discussing this measure for a couple of weeks. To break the discussion at this point, have a debate on agriculture and then return to this debate would mean that in all probability we would have the same series of questions asked over again as are being asked in the present debate.

A day or two ago I asked the house if it would permit us to go into supply -for a few minutes in order to call items in one or two departments so as to enable some other ministers to take up supply on Thursday or Friday and relieve my colleagues who are engaged on war duties for those days. What was the attitude of the opposition to that request? It was to move a

motion on going into supply in the nature of an amendment. An amendment to the motion to go into supply is in the nature of a vote of want of confidence in the government. That would certainly occasion a prolonged debate. What my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is asking us to do is to set aside an important war measure and allow the opposition to say that it has no confidence in the administration, to introduce a vote of want of confidence motion in the house at this time. When it comes to a matter of precedence, I need scarcely say we are not going to give precedence to any measure that has to do with want of confidence in the administration.

speechtext:
Before submitting the estimates of my department, perhaps I should explain to the committee how they are made up.
As hon. members know, the Department of Munitions and Supply is the purchasing branch for the three service departments. We may receive an order for, we will say, a submarine net. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We have heard a great deal about break-downs this afternoon. I am afraid that Britain is going to break down unless we act before it is too late. Let us think about Britain a little more. If she is waiting for Canada to act she will break down. Let us not forget that the whole future of the human race depends upon the battle being fought in Britain now, and we sit here carrying on in this way, with long government statements issued almost every day of the week. I fear for the health of the ministers with all these break-downs. I believe there is a large body of public opinion in this country that is not altogether satisfied with the war policy we are pursuing here, not only the policy of the government but also at times that of the opposition, the alternative government, because as I have said in the past the opposition is also responsible for what goes on in this house, unless it fulfils its functions, as our constitution provides.
I would refer to what happened on July 12 last. Many of us in this house celebrate March 17 and July 12 as the days of two patron saints. Last year we were told that the National Resources Mobilization Act would not be considered on July 12 while we were away, and over fifty soldier members went to Quebec for the week-end. But in the absence of many hon. members the measure was taken up and passed on a Friday, in a very short time. That is how the cumbersome mobilization act came in.
The most important thing in this country to-day is man-power, but as I said a year ago, it is almost as hard for a man to get into the army, the navy or the air force, as it is to get into the exclusive Rideau club. Recruiting is on again, off again and on again, but here we sit hearing essays by ministers, break-downs and all that sort of thing. There have been break-downs all along the line,
and we have been too late in everything. Here we have a total of fifty-four men killed on the highways on account of the lack of free fares, because of the break-down of our railway systems, on which this country has spent hundreds of millions of dollars.
I said yesterday I intended to make only one speech while we are in committee on this matter, and I will conclude in a very few minutes what I have to say to-day. When I mentioned the situation at Camp Borden last week, I had reference to the last war, to 1917.1 admitted that a great many improvements had been made at Borden, but I said I still did not agree with the general camp policy of the government, and this one as a winter camp. But neither then nor at any other time have I cast any reflections on any of the overworked officials or heads of these camps, or members of the cabinet. I realize that they are a government of Canadians in Canada and that it is our duty to cooperate with them to the best of our ability, as long as they are the government, if they get on with the war.
Just here I should like to pay tribute to the permanent officials of the government. I have had a great deal of experience in many spheres of activity, and since coming here in 1921 I have found that the success of any public enterprise and of federal administration depends very largely upon the courteous, able, painstaking, * loyal, sincere but overworked public officials, who d-o their duty splendidly here, and often have to work long hours of overtime. During this war some of them have passed on unwept, unhonoured and unsung, and I wish to pay tribute to the great work being done by these splendid public officials.
Here we have estimates amounting to $1,460,000,000, yet we cannot find a quarter of a million dollars to provide free railway transportation for the soldiers. Here we are proposing to spend $4,000,000 a day on the war, and surely we should be able to devote two and a half hours of that cost, or over $400,000 to this objective of free fares. These boys are risking all; they may be sent to Europe or to Greenland's icy mountains, or as members of the R.C.A.F. they may be killed over Britain or over Berlin. Some of them will never come back, and we have a duty to perform on their behalf. Private members, as well as members of the government have their duties to perform. The only consolation a public man can have, in my view-and I have been in public life a long time-is the comfort in his own conscience that he has done his duty as he saw it to be. I do not want any thanks. As long as I have been a member of parliament I have endeavoured to do my duty, and in doing so I
War Appropriation Bill

have tried never to offend anyone knowingly. Since I have been a member of the House of Commons I have stood for the principles and maintenance of liberties, and I shall continue to do so for the time in the future I may happen to be here.
To-day we are facing the greatest war in the history of the world. I support in this war and the last the cause of those patriots, the private soldiers and men in all ranks, who are doing their duty for their country in this conflict. While I wear the party uniform, I will never wear its plush. I will do my duty in the ranks, but it will as in the past be as a volunteer, not as a conscript. In the past, prior to this war, I have had many differences of opinion with leaders regarding imperial and foreign affairs and defence policies. I am an imperialist. It was said that I was the only one in the house, because I believed that the future freedom, liberty and welfare of the world was in the hands of Great Britain, and depended upon the mother county, on those two little islands on the edge of Europe. The struggle for freedom, liberty and civilization has been made by them, and by them almost alone since France failed, save for the dominions and Greece. Up to this time they have paid on a cash-and-carry basis for all the munitions they have received.
Last year we were dependent upon that glorious country, France, which in the first great war did so much for civilization and freedom. We depended to a great extent upon that great nation and upon the patriotism of the people of France in that war and this. It was with deep regret to the people of the world that France went under. A year ago we were depending upon France to hold the Maginot line until Britain got an army and munitions, and until the dominions could give support with their armies and food and munitions. We found that poor France depended upon us against the dictators in vain. Help did not come in time, through no fault of the mother country. Neither country was ready for war owing to disarmament.
Out on the Pacific coast we are depending upon the United States to protect our western seaboard. We rejoice that they are with us, but I hope their help will not come too late. I have grave doubts about it myself. I fear help is not coming quickly enough. I do not believe the people of 'Canada realize the gravity of the situation, or know to whom this country will belong at the end of 1941. They do not seem to realize that when the war started we had no army, no navy and no air force. We were back to where we were in 1812, a condition of complete dependence upon the mother country for all the freedom of civilization and defence and protection we enjoy.

I should like to make three or four further observations on the subject I was discussing last night at the adjournment. I notice the responsible minister is in his seat to-day, and I am glad to see him because of an editorial which appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail. It is headed, "Help the Soldier Hiker", and states:
But the soldier's uniform is his credential. He is in the king's service; offering his life if necessary for a cause. Military regulations are rigid. Discipline must be maintained. The man who enlists voluntarily in the defence of his country knows all this and soon becomes imbued with the esprit de corps that makes army life a happy memory. Such men do not want to thumb their way along the roads; and they should not fall under the suspicion with which	habitual civilian hitch-hikers	are
regarded.
Then there is an appeal to the citizens to give these men a lift. That is all well and good, and is a good omen.
I may say, however, that on August 6 last I received from the Minister of National Defence a letter in which he uttered the same sentiments. He had a great deal of sympathy for the forces, and replied to me in part in this way in a letter dated August 6:
If occurs to me that in connection with both of these matters there is scope for the activities of our many citizens who want to help in connection with war work, either by means of radio appeals to citizens who are out motoring to give a lift to men in uniform or by means of some arrangement for providing motors at camps or headquarters at certain times, the transportation being in charge of, perhaps, some of our service organizations.
I think myself that this is a worthwhile suggestion, and that it might well be taken up by our citizens if it were brought to their attention. I know .that people are most anxious to help and all they want as suggestion and direction.
I believe if the minister were good enough to let this matter go before the special committee, a programme might be worked out. The railways are making a great deal of money out of 'the war. This programme would involve only 'a small item of expenditure, and I believe the public who would harm to make the payments would be prepared to do so.
Last October 12 to 15, which was the Thanksgiving week-end, I was on the highways. As a result of the condition which obtained at that time, the following editorial appeared on October 15 in 'the Evening Telegram of Toronto;
Motorists travelling south from Barrie and Allandale last Friday and Saturday regretted that Premier King and his ministers could not see the hundreds of soldiers on leave from Camp Borden for the Thanksgiving week-end lining the highway and thumbing their way to their homes in Toronto and elsewhere. The sight of these boys who have volunteered to fight for their country begging rides might

War Appropriation Bill
have awakened the most stolid cabinet member from his complacency and convinced him of the necessity for providing decent, safe and free transportation for soldiers to the larger centres of population.
Even though soldiers can now travel round trip at single trip rates, the railway and bus fares are still beyond the purse of men who are earning only $1.30 a day and assigning part of it to their families. Between Toronto and Barrie the round trip fare for a soldier is $1.95. It is no cheaper for him travelling one way. Consequently he thumbs his way.
This is a cruel situation which might be rectified by a little generosity on the part of the government and some cooperation by the railways who must have idle railway coaches suitable for the short journeys between the military camps and the main transportation transfer points. From these latter the soldiers might be given transportation on the regular schedule trains. Whatever the costs arising from such arrangements they would be infinitesimal in comparison with the enormous expenditures which are now being assumed by the country.
The men in khaki have as good a right to free transportation on the railways as the *thousands of other people who daily ride "dead head" on the trains. The government should give renewed consideration to this question of free transportation for soldiers on leave, not forgetting that the trains are operated anyway, most of them only one-third or one-half full. Railway passes for the soldiers would be an indication that their country appreciates the sacrifices which they are making for it.
I shall conclude what I have to say on this point by reading a telegram I received from Petawawa camp. I do not know why the soldiers write to me, because I do not know as many of them as I used to. Many members from Ontario, travelling on the trains from Ottawa to Toronto, two-t'hirds of whom are government supporters, have an opportunity to speak to soldiers who have been at the Petawawa camp. At the time of the great war an artillery camp was established at that point. It has always been my contention that a camp at Petawawa should not be operative in the winter months.
Here is the telegram which was sent to me yesterday, 'and which I shall be pleased to send to the minister:
Small group Petawawa troops arrested for false railway tickets being used for furloughs and leave. Canadian Pacific Railway pressing charges but only using few soldiers out of hundreds in camp as sole blame same being unfair owing to large scale of sources issuing tickets. Though investigation should strengthen your proposal of free transportation for troops and soldiers. Friend we are in dire need of legal assistance and advice. Can you represent us or assist. Answer collect.
I might say that I sent a return message saying that I was not in a position to appear for them. During the first great war, as the head of the greatest soldier city in Canada, I did appear for them on many occasions.
That is the city to which even to-day they are coming from points as far away as Quebec and sometimes from the west and the maritime provinces to enlist and recruit soldiers and take them out of Toronto. They sent recruits to all parts of this dominion; yet when they asked the minister a year ago to set out the list of Toronto recruits, he could not do it. I wrote asking the number of men enlisted in Toronto, but, no, I could not get that information; it was not listed. I suggest that the department ought to have a proper index filing system which would show the soldier contribution from every municipality in Canada.
In the last war, when the Conservative government was in power, wounded soldiers were arriving in Toronto, and there was a scarcity of hospital accommodation for them or homes to go to. In the dark fall of 1917, during October and November, several hundred soldiers died of the awful flu epidemic, I remember several from Winnipeg and the west who died. I remember one who had been secretary to the late Sir George Bury, who joined the air force. The pool then was at the Jesse Ketchum school in Toronto. Where a man could join the Royal Air Force and be out of the pool in three or four days, now it takes one, two, three or four months as the case may be, at manning pool. This man arrived on Wednesday and he was dead in a week from the flu epidemic.
Having seen this lack of hospital accommodation, I insisted upon a coroner's inquest into this matter and into other cases. This was held and it showed that the government *of the day had not made any arrangements for proper or adequate hospitalization. The suggestion was made that 'the old base hospital on Gerrard street, Toronto, the old Toronto general hospital, should be used. This was closed as not considered fit for civilians, 'but they wanted to turn the key in the door and open it up for soldiers. As a result of that inquest the government spent a large sum of money in providing proper hospitals in every military district. I use this as an illustration of what coroners' inquests can do to get action.
I urge the same thing in connection with soldier fares and this Petawawa case. 1 believe we should do this. I appealed to the attorney general of the province, Mr. Conant, to provide these young men with counsel so that the evidence might be brought out and we might have all the facts, but the attorney general replied that he could not do it because it was only done in capital oases. I suppose they all follow the parliamentarians'
War Appropriation Bill

religion of following the line of leiast resistance. I understand that these men are first offenders. It costs a soldier at Petawawa almost two weeks' pay to buy his fare and berth and meals to make a trip home to Toronto and back. I plead with the minister to consider 'this matter. He has been very sympathetic as I discovered when I first went to see him at his office on his first day as Minister of National Defence. He treated me most courteously. I urge him to have this matter taken up by the select committee which is to consider these expenditures. I believe they could arrive at a reasonable settlement of the question.
Another matter I wish to mention is in connection with guarding city property. I know the Minister of Munitions and Supply will appreciate the problem. Unless we have continuous current and power, these war industries will not be able to work full shifts and production will not be carried on. I believe the government of the day should pay for guarding public property, the same as was done in the last war. They should assume the responsibility of guarding federal, provincial and municipal property. The government is now assuming the responsibility of guarding the power plants at Niagara and other provincial properties and the same thing should be done for the municipalities.
We had a good example of what might happen with the storm of last Tuesday. This storm struck the industrial centres in central Ontario and many power plants were forced temporarily to shut down. For a time elevators were stopped, street-cars could not run and many other activities were shut down for a time because of the storm. The same thing could happen from other causes. The municipalities are not responsible for the war, nor is it their duty to maintain armed forces. In 1940 it cost the city of Toronto $325,000 to guard power plants and other public property. The government has agreed to protect provincial property, so why not municipal property? The municipalities have no more right to pay for the guarding of public property than they have to pay the militia for the defence of Canada. Under the British North America Act matters concerning militia and defence are exclusively within federal jurisdiction. There is no necessity for the government to act the part of what judges and lawyers refer to as dead-beats so far as the municipalities are concerned, in paying for guards to protect power plants which supply current to munition plants.
If these power plants are shut down; if power fails, even for a few hours, it will be impossible to turn out munitions. Why do the government not adopt the same principle

for the municipalities as they have adopted in connection with the provinces? During the last war the munition plants of Ontario at one time turned out fifty-five per cent of the shells, owing to cheap hydro power, yet the dominion most unjustly and unpatriotically made the hydro pay over $1,500,000 in customs duties on factory and generator equipment for the building of the Chippawa plant, which took three years to build. To supply power for munitions, Ottawa should do its duty. At least some part of this appropriation should be spent in protecting these public plants. That would be far better than spending $378,000 upon our legations the world over, and $125,000 upon the League of Nations, when nobody knows where it is. It has been lost, strayed or stolen.
One power plant, the hydro-electric distribution system in Toronto, supplies all the munitions plants in the district with power. An interruption in supply of power from any one of the vital generating plants or transmission facilities will cut off a major block of power and shut down for many months essential industries engaged in the manufacture of war materials. The dominion government is already providing military protection to transportation w'orks and to a large number of private industries. It would not only be more economical but just and necessary to extend this same military protection to the power plants and distribution systems which provide and will continue to provide if protected, electrical energy to those industries manufacturing war munitions and war materials so vital to Canada's best contribution in this present war.
I view with alarm the present extremely costly and inefficient methods of providing civilian protection to electrical plants, which duty has been forced upon the municipalities and the province of Ontario. I feel that more effective means of guarding these vital facilities can be effected by the dominion government using the militia now in training without any additional expense to the taxpayers, and with the added advantage of giving valuable practical experience to the militia. That would be far better than having sixty men guarding the Royal Canadian Air Force property at the foot of Yonge street. These men are on guard twenty-four hours a day, in all kinds of weather. Yet there is already triple protection for this property, by the city police, by the harbour commission and by the contractor. Anyone who is travelling on a train leaving Toronto can see this long row of buildings and realize that it would be far better to have only five or six guards.
The hydro commission respectfully urges that the dominion government immediately take over and supply all necessary protection

War Appropriation Bill
for all vital hydro electric and public utility plants and power distribution systems in the saipe way as they were guarded during the great war and as is now being done in many cases for private industry. This is a splendid statement from the local municipal system.
There is another matter I should like to bring up, one which I do not think has been mentioned before in this debate. How does it come that everything is as usual in this country? If this committee would visit some of the large cities during the week-ends, they would see that everything is going on as usual. A visit to department stores or various places of entertainment in any city will show no evidence that Canada is at war. All that can be seen is a few soldiers on the streets, otherwise everything is just as usual, in this country. How are we going to fight Hitler that way? Why are we always talking about break-downs and all that kind of thing? Let us admit now that unless we give more urgent aid to Britain, it is possible that Britain may break down. I hope the committee will visit different centres of population and see for themselves that everything is as usual.
I want to turn now to the question of national soldiers' insurance. This country has money to provide insurance for those civilians who stay at home, but it proposes to do nothing in the way of providing insurance for those who are prepared to give their lives in defence of this country. To them it gives $1.30 a day, and orit of that they have to find their own pocket-money and fares. I appreciate the hard work which the war ministers and the leader of the opposition are doing. I have always found them courteous in replying to a private member of parliament and they are willing to give freely of their time when a member writes to them. I am glad to pay this tribute to them and the leader of the opposition. But I do say that when this country can pay to insure those who stay at home, it should be able to insure those who are risking their lives for civilization.
During the great war the city of Toronto insured every one of its soldiers for $1,000. I have here the report of George Wilson, commissioner of finance, dealing with the matter. He says:
In November, 1914, the city decided to purchase-at its own cost-insurance coverage for all citizens of Toronto who enlisted for overseas service. Under such plan, 9,609 $1,000 insurance policies were purchased during the period November, 1914, to May. 1915, at a premium cost to the city of $1,247,261. As the city in May, 1915, was unable to obtain further insurance cover from local insurance companies, provincial legislation was applied for and granted, under which the city itself became
the insurer of all citizens who thereafter enlisted for active service. In all cases, whether the citizens were insured by companies or by the city under the legislation referred to, the city was appointed beneficiary with power to administer the losses under such policy. Under the plan, which became effective in 1915. approximately 35,400 citizens enlisted for active service overseas; all claims under such insurance scheme being paid by the city. The total number of death claims paid by the city was 4.904-which cost the city $4,378,020.
To be eligible for the insurance, a soldier had to have lived in the city two years, and a great many had not lived there that long and therefore did not qualify for the insurance. Another qualification was that they had to have someone dependent upon them. The report goes on to say:
The cost of guards for protection of city properties, that is, water works pumping stations, sewage disposal plants, et cetera, during the war 1914-1918 totalled $442,000. No contribution to such cost was made by the federal government.
Re protection of city properties since war was declared September 3, 1939. The expenditures from September 3 last to date-approximately 12 weeks-has cost the city approximately $88,000.
In this connection let me point out that if they had not enlisted for this tvar many of our soldiers who have been killed on the highways would have been alive to-day, and they get no pension at all when they are killed in an accident, even though they have a pass from Camp Borden and are on military duty. A moral responsibility rests on the nation to insure the soldier against road accidents. Insurance could be taken out for 25 cents a week. Some of the insurance companies in this country are trying to push the sale of insurance to soldiers, using as an argument that they may be disabled and prevented from purchasing insurance on their return from the war. After the last war insurance was made available to our soldiers, and I think the government should make a statement of its policy in this regard. Mr. Finlayson, superintendent of insurance, in a letter to me said with reference to my proposal for government insurance of enlisted men:
Our conclusion is that the government's obligation to returning men and to the dependents of men dying in the service can best be discharged through the provisions of the Pension Act, which deals with the claims of soldiers or dependents in accordance with the need and the facts of the particular case. Government schemes of insurance are necessarily of general application and result in unnecessary insurance in some cases and entirely inadequate amounts in others. The result is that, notwithstanding such insurance, the pension problem remains in practically undiminished importance and, since the needs must be met in part by the pension provision, it is preferable to deal with the whole problem in that way. The further arguments which
War Appropriation Bill

have seemed to us to inevitably lead to this conclusion need not be stated here, but I shall be glad to discuss them with you after you arrive in Ottawa, if you so desire.
We should have a national scheme of insurance for soldiers which would also provide for the soldier when he comes back from the war, provide against lack of employment, reconstruction days, disability and many other hazards. It would effect an economy.
The United States had a system of soldier insurance during the great war. I think the amount of the insurance was $5,000, and with the premium charge that was made for it, this scheme was found to effect a great economy in their pension bill. I have a letter here from Mr. Stimson, Secretary for War in the United States, enclosing a copy of their new national insurance scheme for soldiers. I have received a great many applications for copies of it and I would ask the minister to allow it to be placed on the record; it is only three or four short pages long. It shows the present national scheme of insurance for soldiers in the United States. Have the ministers any objection to allowing the members to see this national scheme of insurance? It is contained in circular No. 125 from the War Department, Washington, approved by the president, dated October 31, 1940.

I repeat that I do not want any favours, and if letting hon. members know what is done elsewhere is a favour I say no; I would rather not have it. As I was saying, I believe that the principle of the War Measures Act has been extended to rents. It should be extended to cover shark small loan companies, and their rates curtailed. The other day I was in a building where there were a number of soldiers, poor women and children complaining that this act had not been enforced. It should be enforced, and there should be a national moratorium all along the line on interest mortgage rates, as I proposed last June, to five per cent.
One other matter. I understand that the Minister of Munitions and Supply has established a national industrial commission, with offices and staff, no doubt, at a large cost. I should like to find out what are their functions and duties, and the estimated cost of the commission. Does it aim at decentralization of industry, and how, or regulation of location? Who is asking for such a board, and on whose advice has it been decided to establish it? Will all letters, correspondence and other data relating thereto be tabled? What are the factors which determine a proper plant location? Has the minister or have his officials passed any rules or regulations in this respect, and, if so, what are they? From the experience I have had, I may say that there are more than adequate sources of information and advice in this country to assist any competitive industry which seeks a location. Decentralization is a meaningless term as applied to industry. It has been proved in

War Appropriation Bill
the United States and in Canada that the simple laws of supply and demand of labour, materials and markets are constantly adjusting the location of competitive industry to its most advantageous area. When these laws are interfered with, nothing but trouble results.

speechtext:
I want to say a very few words in reply to the criticism by the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) of certain statements made by me in this chamber on Monday last. But before doing that, I will make two observations. First, I wish to tell the minister that in raising the points which I put forward on Monday I had no other thought than to help to promote the greatest cooperation among the various forces in the country, in order that victory may crown our efforts. Second, I wish to tell the minister that I did not by any means exhaust the resources I could draw upon to establish more firmly, if necessary, the points I raised on that occasion.
I think the minister's criticism of yesterday was exceedingly weak. The first point he raised was that I had proposed or suggested the amalgamation of the Department of Labour
with the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I did nothing of the kind. What I did suggest was that the Department of Munitions and Supply should keep its hands off the affairs of the Department of Labour, and I told the Minister of Labour that he ought to be master in his own house. If the information I have from various labour organizations is correct, it is there that the chief difficulty between the Department of Labour and labour organizations at the present time exists. If the minister had taken note of the criticism made in this regard at the trades and labour congress convention at Vancouver in September last, he would realize, as I believe he does, that strong exception is taken by organized labour throughout the country to the interference by the Department of Munitions and Supply in matters which are purely within the province of the Department of Labour.
The minister indicated a number of ways in which, in his opinion, the government is cooperating with labour. He first mentioned that the government had set up the war-time prices and trade board. What connection has that with cooperation with labour? We all know the purposes of the establishment of that board, and certainly it was not created just to benefit the labour movement.
He then referred to the number of positions given to labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Surely that has nothing to do with what we were talking about. The posts which were allotted to labour under that act represented merely the division of the administrative positions as between employers and labour. That is definitely provided for in the act; it was in the act of 1935; and it is irrelevant for the minister to bring up the matter at this time in order to try to throw discredit on the points I raised.
Then he went on to say that Tom Moore, president of the trades and labour congress, would be offered the chairmanship of the national employment committee which is to be created by the unemployment insurance commission. I am sure that I am as pleased as is the minister that such an appointment is intended for Mr. Moore, because I do not know of any man more capable than he is to discharge the duties of that office, and I hope he can see his way clear to take it. But it is a matter which has nothing to do with the questions I raised on Monday.
He then referred to order in council No. 2685, passed in June, in which the government laid down the principles which it maintained should obtain as between employers and employed. The position which labour takes in this matter is that employers do not pay any attention whatever to those principles, and even the government itself, when doing certain
War Appropriation Bill

works, forgets that it passed the order. As a matter of fact, last summer the government abrogated the Fair Wages and Hours of Work Act on a certain work after passing this order and without consulting in any way with the labour supply council. I pointed that out in the house last November. Last Monday I quoted from the Canadian Congress Journal, showing that what I was saying was not merely my own opinion but the opinion of those who were in a position to speak for labour. Let me read the last paragraph of an editorial in which reference to the national labour supply council is made. This is from the Canadian Congress Journal of February, 1941:
The weakness of the national labour supply council is that it has not been allowed to function as a planning body, but instead, merely called upon to give an advisory opinion, many times at extremely short notice, on measures already prepared by others. To be of real use, workers' representatives should be placed in a position where they can contribute from their experience toward the shaping of policies and not be called into consultation only after the course of action has been decided upon.

First, this is not my statement. Second, I would assume that the Canadian Congress Journal would know what it was talking about when it made this statement. If there has been a solitary case of consultation on their owu initiative, the exception only proves the rule. I have been watching the relations between the government and the national labour supply council ever since it was set up; I have been more or less in touch with some of those who are on it, and if I may be allowed to use a homely simile to express what I think of it, the relation seems to me something like a number of gentiles inviting a Jew to lunch and giving him pork chops. He has to do the best he can in the circumstances; he has to cut off the fat and other things to make them as palatable as possible to his psychological stomach and then either eat them or throw them out of the window. That is the position of labour in fifty per cent of the cases with the national labour supply council. As the editorial states, they are called into consultation only after the course of action has been decided upon.
I have in my hand an article by A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour, on the government's wage policy.

This article appeared in the Canadian Unionist of January, 1941. There was so much criticism of order in council 7440, that the president of the Canadian Congress of Labour decided it was necessary to reply and show the position that labour was really in. He stated:
I feel therefore that it would be desirable to explain why the order in council was approved, and why I believe that if properly applied it will be helpful rather than harmful to the interests of the workers. We should all realize that very great pressure is being used by certain interests in Canada at the present time to rob organized labour of its hard-won rights and to prevent it from extending its organization. It is therefore possible-
I ask hon. members to note this.
-that had not this order in council been approved, something very much more severe and harmful to the interests of the workers might have been passed.
In other words, A. R. Mosher, who, I believe, is a member of the national labour supply council, was handed the pork chop and he realized that if he did not eat it he might be given dog.
Then reference was made to the question of the turnover at the Malton plant. I gave certain figures, the result of an investigation,- not official-made of conditions in the Malton plant. I am sure that if I read even half of that report, it would create a furore throughout the country. The point is, however, it is admitted that labour conditions in the Malton plant are such that they are interfering with production. That is something that the minister cannot gloss over. Speaking in this committee on February 28, the Minister of Munitions and Supply made some reference to the Malton plant, and he was asked these questions, as reported on page 1137 of Hansard:
Mr. Coldwell: Does the minister not think that the big labour turnover in Malton is a factor ?
Mr. Howe: Certainly it is. It is a reflection on something.
Mr. Coldwell: Can the minister tell us why there is such a large turnover?
Mr. Howe: I cannot. We have been trying without success to find out the reason. In 1936, there was practically no aeroplane industry in Canada; I suppose it was employing less than one thousand men; to#-day it is employing twenty thousand.
Mr. Maclnnis: Did the minister approach the employees at Malton to try to get their point of view?
Mr. Howe:	No, I have enough trouble
approaching the management.
That, as I said the other day, gives an insight into this whole matter of employer-labour relations as far as the government's attitude is concerned. When the Minister of Labour wanted to get further information, he merely asked the company what the turnover was and they said so much per cent, but only for the last six months.

I was referring to the
information I had at the time. As a matter of fact, I had it before the house met in November, but the whole position was so serious that, in view of the situation, we decided to leave the matter for the time being, in the hope that perhaps it could be approached in some other way.
Then there was the question of the company entirely disregarding the regulations of the government re wages. The minister adroitly sidestepped all the major issues; he referred to the matter of sanitary conditions and said that that was under provincial jurisdiction, and of course this government could not do anything about it. I am getting rather tired of this buck passing with regard to what the government may or may not do. I wish to tell the minister and the government that they have complete control and complete power in the matter of war contracts and
government contracts generally. They give a contract; they can stipulate the conditions and wages which must be observed under that contract. In the United States they are imposing upon industrial organizations as a condition of getting any contract, that the company concerned must live up to the provisions of the Wagner labour act. Just recently the Henry Ford company was refused a contract to supply $10,000,000 worth of equipment until such time as it would agree to respect the conditions imposed in the Wagner act.
Then the minister referred to the matter of finger-printing at the Fairchild plant. I have letters from employees in this plant, but I am not going to take time to place them on record because the matter has already been discussed. The minister said that the finger-printing had been done, all right, but that it was voluntary. Surely he is not so naive as to think anything remains voluntary when a man has to have a job in order to live. Just supposing that the minister and I, if we were capable of doing that sort of work, went to the Fairchild plant, filled out application forms, were accepted and told to go to work; then the person taking our application said, "Well, Mr. McLarty, Miss Jones will take your fingerprints."
Mr. MeLARTY: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman again, but perhaps his remark is made as the result of a misunderstanding for which I do not blame him, because the report in Hansard was not one as complete as that I intended to give. The purpose of the finger-printing at the Fairchild plant, I am informed by the manager and I have not gone into it further, was that in the event of sabotage or accident, in connection with men badly injured or perhaps killed, this was the best method of their identification. Let me be fair about it. I do not think the hon. member would draw that deduction from my remarks as reported in Hansard, and in that event perhaps it is my fault; but finger-printing is for that purpose. It is not for any policing purpose; it is a purely voluntary undertaking, providing a convenient method of identification in the event of injury or death as the result of sabotage. I do not, however, blame my hon. friend for taking the meaning that he has taken.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
accept the minister's explanation; and, although usually I do not like to see people hard-boiled, I am glad he did not take the other point of view. But suppose it is for that purpose; why have a voluntary fingerprinting policy or system? If it is to be of

War Appropriation Bill

any value at all, it should be compulsory. After all, in the case of sabotage the man who intended to commit sabotage would refuse to have his finger-prints taken, while the man who did not care, the man whose heart and mind were open, would say, "I am quite willing to have my finger-prints taken; it does not matter." The voluntary idea does not really stand at all.
Then there was the matter of the application for the board at the plant of the National Steel Car Corporation. I am quite aware of the circumstances mentioned yesterday by the minister, and I believe and know that his department has done and is doing excellent work in settling difficulties that arise between employers and their working staffs. There is not the slightest doubt in the world that this is so. I think under the late Mr. Rogers great advances were made in that direction, and I hope and believe that the work done by him is being carried on under the present minister. But in order to support my point I should like to quote again from the memorandum presented to this government by the Canadian Congress of Labour on February 14, 1941. Under the heading "The Right of Association," section 5 of the memorandum states:
The congress desires to commend the government for its action in setting forth in order in council P.C. 2685 a statement of principles for the regulation of labour conditions during the war. . . .
I am not completing that sentence; the remainder is not important. I want to point this out, however, so that I may not be accused of taking something from its context. That is perfectly satisfactory, and I am in agreement with it. Then the memorandum goes on:
It is pointed out, however, that many employers, including those who have obtained huge war orders from the government, are refusing to respect these principles, and are using every means in their power to prevent the workers from being organized. They are unwilling to meet committees representing their employees, and endeavour in many instances to set up so-called "company unions" under tlieir control, in direct contravention of the principles quoted above. At its convention in September last, the congress approved a resolution that the government be asked to use its authority under the War Measures Act to ensure that its labour policy be observed by all employers in their relationships with their workers.
Then section 7 goes on:
The difficulties involved in enforcing the principles enunciated by the government upon recalcitrant employers are recognized, but so long as no action is taken to insist upon their acceptance, the order in council is of little or no value to the workers, who are themselves carefully observing it. Can they not see that the safety of the nation, the maintaining of democracy, depends upon the spreading of control and administration over as large a proportion of the people as possible.
A shattering revolution took place in Russia in 1917. That revolution came almost entirely because of the suppression of the common people in that country, the suppression of generations of peasants and workers by successive governments. In France the large employers of labour were hostile to their employees; the result w'as that communism was much more general in labour unions in that country than it was in Great Britain, where for generations labour organizations have been recognized. I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser) yesterday afternoon. He suggested, as did the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), that it would be a good thing if members of this house visited some of the plants engaged in war work. I have visited several of these plants, but I have an idea just how much information an ordinary member would get, and how difficult he would find it to ascertain whether or not the plant was operating properly, whether or not it was doing its best, and so on. He would have a great deal of difficulty in finding out these things, I believe, unless he was given the information by the management, and in many of these plants the management is rather diffident about giving out such information. Hon. members here have to depend upon information which they receive from various people interested in certain industries.
To-night I should like to say a few more words about the aircraft industry, to the early difficulties of w'hieh the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, referred yesterday. He felt that the industry was entitled to some sort of defence, and I agree. When we consider the difficulties with which aircraft production in Canada has been faced; when we consider all that is necessary in order to produce aeroplanes, some of which have fifty thousand parts, the aeroplane manufacturers of this country are to be commended for what they have achieved. They should be praised also for their initiative and foresight in connection with various enterprises. We all know that this is a mushroom industry, with very little background, as the United States: expert said, although some of these plants did have some experience.
Two or three matters come to mind in connection with the production of aeroplanes in Canada. We must give credit to Associated Aircraft for the vision, foresight and perseverance they showed as far back as 1938. We also know that the industry has been hampered because of difficulties in securing certain secret processes and patents and designs. I know that in 1937 one concern, having in mind that at some future time it might become difficult to obtain a certain alloy which was essential in the manufacture of aeroplanes, put experts to work and discovered

War Appropriation Bill
the composition, of this alloy. To-day the whole industry is reaping the benefit of the work done by that company. I mention this incident in order to show that some firms in Canada have at least some little background along this line. Certainly they all have more background and more experience than Federal Aircraft. Considering everything, I believe these older firms have done fairly well, and it might be a good idea for the government to have a few conferences with them and follow some of their recommendations.
Most of us are greatly disappointed because the production of aeroplanes in this country has not been up to schedule, but there have been many difficulties in connection with designs, in getting parts, in obtaining machine tools, and so on. The minister said that in some instances the output of finished planes was very disappointing indeed. During the course of his remarks he said he thought they should have done better, and I believe he suggested that 'in certain instances the management was not all that it should be. While there may have been some faults on the part of the management, I do not think the minister has been quite fair. Is it not a fact that there is a multiplicity of control over supplies, over inspection and over the delivery of component parts, matters which are beyond the jurisdiction of the contractors themselves? It is directly the responsibility of some department of government to see that these things are delivered. Those are matters which are beyond the control of the contractors.
There are three separate authorities in the administration of aircraft construction. There are three separate authorities interested in checking costs. There were two separate gov-erment inspection organizations; I do not know whether that has been changed. There are three separate groups active in obtaining materials and equipment. All of the above are in addition to the organization of the contractor who, under any circumstances, must operate under each of the above sections.
I have in my hand a partial list of aircraft contracts in progress in Canada. This partial list illustrates clearly the question of control, and I should like to place it on Hansard. The list of aircraft, and the comments, are shown in the accompanying table.
It will be noted that in respect of the Noorduyn Aviation Company Limited, Mr. MacMillan said, in his report, that the manufacturing technique of that plant is the farthest advanced of any plant in Canada, and that unless they are held up by the nonreceipt of ordered material or components, they will complete their contract. He gives them a good record. However, the multiplicity of control with respect to some of the M873-96}
others is easily seen in the list I have placed on record. It is apparent that in some instances production is not as good as it might be, and I am wondering whether that multiplicity of control has anything to do with that condition.
As I said earlier, it is at once apparent that where there was simple control there was good progress, but where control was complicated the progress was not as good. Is it not fundamental that the only service required from the aircraft industry is the reasonably economic production of aircraft, with all possible speed? Normal activities are necessarily divided into two main requirements: (1) the operation of aircraft production plants involving the fabrication of raw materials and their assembly with aircraft equipment and accessories into complete aircraft, by the use of labour and (2) an assured flow of all supplies required by the production plants. These supplies comprise raw materials, aircraft equipment and accessories, production equipment and labour sufficiently trained to be readily absorbed in the work. Then, to operate under wartime emergency conditions, a third requirement becomes essential, namely, the coordination of the industry to form a unit of production, in order to obtain and make possible efficiency in output.
Under normal conditions a contractor undertakes, as his function of management, the fulfilment of the first two requirements. But with the present demand for very rapid expansion if the contractor-management is permitted free access to the various markets involved, the industry will suffer from uneconomical distribution of supplies, leading directly to decreased gross production and increased gross cost. Also, a general scramble for contracts instead of allocation of work means overloading of the successful scramblers, and something less than full use of other facilities. The function of management can be fulfilled most efficiently by the operation of each plant on productive work for which it is best suited, and if the supply problem is undertaken by the government, the full energy of management can be concentrated on plant operation and supervision of labour.
With the present congestion of markets for all aircraft materials and production equipment, efficient operation is possible only by authoritative coordination and allocation of the available supplies, while training of labour can best be centralized and controlled by direct governmental action. It will be clear that a vigorous reorganization of the control of the aircraft industry is badly needed.

I think we can easily understand the delay which has been caused by the Department of National Defence for Air. They want to have everything up to the last minute. He said that in some training schools three advanced training planes were doing the work of four because there had been delays in the Canadian production of these planes. The minister then went on to say:
Unfortunately I do not know why it has not been possible to produce these planes on schedule and I am not in a position to judge the delays, but one exasperated officer did tell me the other day that there are some manufacturers who were either damn fools or damn liars.
Why was that statement made? The minister wanted to impress the people of Canada with the necessity for airmen. Then in his speech he warned the people against complacency. In addition, the result of the activities of the past year in relation to the vast sums of money expended and contracts let, has created a great deal of disappointment in the public mind. Is it any wonder, then, that there is widespread doubt and scepticism with regard to the efficiency of direction and the general effectiveness of the government's efforts?
The minister has raised the question of shortage of labour. May I call his attention to the fact that the present government was in power during the time when labour was rusting and rotting through lack of facilities which the government ought to have provided to enable these men to remain efficient. These men were not only unemployed, but forced by the complacency and lack of constructive measures of this government to become unemployables. Returned veterans in their forties and fifties are not the least among those compelled to remain idle during that period, and are now numbered among those who are termed "unemployable".
During this long period the government were lacking not only in inclination but also in vision, and made no effort, or no effective effort, to grapple with this problem. They contented themselves with providing mere sustenance for those hundreds of thousands who, through no fault of their own, were forced to accept charity, instead of the work they were eagerly seeking. The minister of munitions is now an apologist for the utter neglect of these unemployables by his own government during the three years before the war.
Now that they are looking for skilled men, the government have created machinery in the form of an unemployment insurance commission, having as its object the care of the unemployed during the period wherein there is an actual scarcity of skilled labour. May I recall the fact that a similar measure was enacted by the Bennett government in 1935. The present government, however, preferred to fight this act in the courts, even up to the privy council, to prove that it was unconstitutional, rather than do the obvious and proper thing which they should have done if they were sincerely interested in the welfare of the working man, namely, secure the consent of the provinces and the British government to make this act constitutional. At that time of unprecedented unemployment a measure such as this would have been of the

There was also the problem of young men leaving school, for whom there was no vocational training adequate to fit them for a job requiring skill. In addressing this committee last Monday afternoon, I undertook to set forth some of Germany's methods of financing the war. Many people throughout Canada, and particularly in my province of Alberta, have been urging strongly that we should look to Germany and adopt some of her methods. I have, therefore, undertaken an examination of Germany's methods and wish to make a few more observations on them.
At that time I pointed out that in Germany more than one-third of the revenue, nearly one-half, was being raised by taxation, and quite a large part of the revenue has been raised by borrowing. They get a great deal of revenue by selling loot from countries that they have overrun. They are printing money very freely for use outside Germany in buying goods from the small nations that are afraid to refuse to sell goods to them. Within Germany their currency is fairly stable owing to fixed prices and control.
I now wish to read from the last report made by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance. It is dated February, 1941. In this report the governor of the bank says:
The truth is that German monetary policy has not been unusual. It has been simply an easy money policy of the sort which has been followed in many countries during the past decade. In Canada, for example, between January, 1933, and August, 1939, the total volume of money (i.e. coin, notes and bank deposits) was increased by some $750,000,000. International comparisons of the volume of money cannot be pushed too far since the velocity of circulation is an important factor, but it may be worth noting that on a per capita basis, the increase in the volume of money was about the same in Canada as it was in Germany, over the pre-war period. As for 14873-97
the period since the war began, the available information suggests that the volume of money has been increased considerably less in Germany than it has been in Canada, on a per capita comparison.
A realistic appraisal of nazi monetary policy must, of course, take account of the very complete and rigorous system of direct controls which the rulers of Germany have imposed upon their people. For example, nearly every article of consumption is rationed, wage levels and farm prices are rigidly pegged down, and the operations of private business are "supervised" in minute detail. With such controls in operation, the immediate danger involved in an unduly large increase in the volume of money would obviously be less than it would be if the controls did not exist. The fact that the nazis did not resort to issuing new money on an exaggerated scale is all the more significant in view of the margin of safety which they might have expected their elaborate direct controls to provide.
The policies which have been described above are those followed within the reich. In the occupied territories, on the other hand, the nazis have used the printing press deliberately as a means of plundering those areas. Instead of seizing goods the Germans simply bought them, paying with newly printed notes, and the people were robbed of purchasing power by soaring prices. This refined method of looting tends to hide the nazis' responsibility for resulting scarcities, and bears most heavily on sections of the population least able to endure it, thus helping to disrupt the economy and destroy the unity of the conquered people.
Hitler and his economic advisers have been most careful to avoid anything in the nature of inflation within Germany. Observers who have visited Germany tell us that Germany is fearful of another inflation; the people remember only too well the great inflation of 1923 and are fearful of a repetition of it.
Nazi war economy is based upon two factors: one being efficient exploitation of German labour and industry, achieved through crushing taxation, forced loans and ruthless regimentation of labour and capital.
The people of Canada will stand for heavy taxation; they may stand for forced loans, but I doubt very much if they would stand for the ruthless regulation of labour and capital that prevails in Germany. The Minister of Finance, in discussing this matter on November 21 last, used these words:
The whole habits of thought of the Canadian people, the dislike of intensive and general government intervention in their personal transactions and private affairs, would make a universal system of price fixing and rationing, even if it were practicable in Canada, far more odious, I am satisfied, than a system of taxation and borrowing out of savings, which is the policy of this government. Every detail of our economic life would have to be controlled by someone sitting here in Ottawa.
I do not believe the people of Canada would stand for such rigid control.

War Appropriation Bill

The other factor in nazi war economy is an equally efficient and systematic exploitation of conquered countries, achieved by confiscation of foodstuffs, military supplies, raw materials and industrial facilities by forced labour and disguised robbery practised by the circulation of worthless currency. Hitler's first method is open to us if we are prepared to make the sacrifice; but currency inflation and social credit remedies have nothing to do with Hitler's success and can contribute nothing to our effort.

No doubt the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat intended his remarks, the last time he spoke, particularly for the benefit of the group with which I am associated, and no doubt he is expecting some comment from this comer. I think, however, it sufficient to say that I do not believe his argument needs any comment. I believe he has done a perfect job of refuting his own argument; consequently it requires no refutation from this corner. For example, the hon. member in his speech the other day suggested that we in this comer have advocated financial methods which do not involve increased taxation and increased borrowing. Then he proceeded to prove that Germany has used practically nothing but taxation and borrowing methods, and he drew his conclusion in this sentence:
Apart from taxation, most of Germany's financing has been done by borrowing.
I think it should be obvious to anyone that the hon. gentleman has refuted his own argument, and it requires no further comment. With regard, however, to the subject of the financial methods to be used in connection with Canada's war effort, if the hon. gentleman will keep his ears open I think I can supply him with all the information he desires as to the social credit point of view.
I dislike being critical, and I wish circumstances to-day were such that I would feel obliged to present the government with one verbal bouquet after another. I have, however, sat here patiently and have listened carefully to all the criticism that has been offered with regard to government policies, not only by the opposition but by supporters of the government as well; and I must say that, as a result, from the point of view from which I wish to discuss this measure, I cannot be anything but critical of the government's policy. I say that notwithstanding what was said the other night by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) with regard to the duty of members

of parliament to develop a war spirit and morale in this country of ours. At page 1442 of Hansard the minister made this statement:
We have a lot to be thankful for in this country, and very little to grouse about after all

I agree with the minister that we have a lot to be thankful for, and we are thankful. We in the opposition are just as thankful as the minister is, and I believe that applies to the people of Canada also. We admire the British people for the courage they have shown in meeting the dangers with which they are faced, and I am sure all the people of Canada will gladly make all the necessary sacrifices they may yet be called upon to make in this great struggle. Nevertheless I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that to compare conditions in Canada with conditions in Britain certainly is no answer to the criticisms that have been offered as to government policy. To say that we ought to be satisfied with unnecessarily unsatisfactory conditions in Canada because the British people are in daily fear of their lives is, in my opinion, illogical reasoning. To say that we ought to tolerate poverty and insecurity in the presence of not only potential but actual abundance in this country appears to me to be the height of inconsistency. I should like to tell the minister candidly that I think his basis of comparison is entirely wrong. What we should be comparing is the conditions that could obtain in this country as contrasted with those that do obtain to-day. I consider this the only fair basis of comparison.
The minister spoke of developing a war spirit and strengthening the morale of both the civil and soldier population of Canada. I agree entirely that this is essential; but surely it must occur to the minister that the most effective way of creating a stronger morale and war spirit is to see that the people of this country get justice. I am satisfied that if, in Canada, every available man-hour were being used, at remunerative wages, and if conditions were such as are physically possible, there would be very, very little by way of criticism of government policy, either from the people or from the opposition in this house.
So far as government policy is concerned, I believe there are some obvious inconsistencies in the statements which have been made by the various ministers, and I should like to draw attention to statements of policy by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). On several occasions we have heard

War Appropriation Bill
the Minister of Finance state that the only limit to be imposed upon Canada's war effort was the physical, mental and moral capacity of Canadians to bear burdens. I believe that is almost exactly the statement made by the minister. Personally I agree that this is the limit of what Canada can do. On the other hand we have the Minister of Munitions and Supply saying that we are unable to do certain things because we cannot afford the cost. As reported at page 916 of Hansard, when the matter of building ships on the Pacific coast was under discussion, in replying to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) the Minister of Munitions and Supply made this statement:
No one is more anxious than I am to distribute plants, but when a study of plants is made, either for British account or for Canadian account, there are certain requirements that must be taken into consideration, and one of these is power-the source and the cost of power.
I am rather at a loss to understand what the Minister of Munitions and Supply means when he suggests that one point to be taken into consideration is "the cost of power." Surely he cannot mean that we are lacking in the physical cost required to set up power plants and to develop power. Obviously he must have had reference to the financial cost.
On the one hand, the Minister of Finance contends that there is to be no limiting in the financial realm, and that the only limitations to be imposed are physical; yet, on the other, we have the Minister of Munitions and Supply stating that we cannot build ships because of the costs involved. Obviously there is an inconsistency between the statements of policy of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
If we can judge from the last words in the recent speech of the British Prime Minister, upon which occasion he concluded with a plea for the tools of war, certainly materials are needed. If those materials are needed and we in Canada can provide them physically, surely we ought to provide them, regardless of how much effort and physical material go into their production. Yet the Minister of Munitions and Supply has said that we must consider the cost. I say to the government that unless Canada is making use of every available man-hour and every ounce of material, Canada is not making her maximum war effort. I challenge any of the ministers, . including the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Munitions and Supply, to refute that contention. I believe very little examination and effort is required to find that Canada 14873-97}
is falling far short of what she is capable of doing, either in her war effort or in her domestic effort.
We have corroboration from the government side of the house, as well as the opposition side, for the contention that there are thousands of man-hours available in Canada- yes, literally thousands of man-hours going: to waste. Nevertheless the government has the-effrontery through its ministers to contend in the House of Commons that Canada is making her maximum effort. Furthermore, much more training of unskilled labour could be done. If these labourers are not required in industries, certainly they should at this time be prepared to take their place in industrial occupations. If we should happen to run short of manpower, surely it would be a simple matter to obtain help from across the boundary line, where they have many thousands of idle men.
In addition, we have available an enormous number of man-hours in undeveloped water power. At a point later in my speech I shall place on Hansard some statistics to indicate our great potential resources of electrical energy which have not been put to use. In passing, however, may I point to some statements which have been made by hon. members on the government and opposition sides of the house which would indicate that we certainly can afford the real cost of making a great contribution to the war effort, and at the same time take care of our domestic requirements.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck)
is reported as follows at page 858:
It seems to me that the nervousness over this proposed appropriation arises from the fact that we are talking in terms of money instead of in terms of goods produced. That is why fear grips the hearts of many people and why we are wondering whether this effort will be successful.
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) made reference to the speech of the hon. member for Trinity, and made this further observation, as reported at page 1309 of Hansard:
The war appropriation bill now before the committee of the whole contains figures so enormous that sometimes one is likely to conclude that such figures are beyond the human resources of this nation. In the early days of this debate the hon. member for Trinity explained forcefully how these figures mean very little. He pointed out that, after all, only goods and services really matter, and that it is goods and services which constitute the real wealth of this nation.
Then this point is made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), as reported at page 918 of Hansard:
I am told there is no reason why we could not be building at least fifty merchant vessels on that coast. At the present moment I believe there are contracts for eight.
